forces: Flute, oboe, clarinet, horn and bassoon
performers: Wind Quintet of the Royal Orchestra, Copenhagen (Det Kgl. Kapels Blæserkvintet): Holger Gilbert-Jespersen, flute; Svend Christian Felumb, oboe; Aage Oxenvad, clarinet; Hans Sørensen, horn; Knud Lassen, bassoon
intro: The Menuet of Nielsen’s Wind Quintet has a clarinet melody over a staccato bassoon, a Trio in F major and a short Coda. This side was re-recorded on 5 May 1936, more than three months after the rest of the quintet was made for HMV in Copenhagen.

sections.label: A′ · Menuet returns, written out
sections.mNote: Bar 72 repeats the opening texture, clarinet over bassoon.

cues.title: Menuet, clarinet and bassoon
cues.text: The Menuet is in 3/4, marked ♩ = 96. The clarinet plays the melody at mp over staccato repeated notes in the bassoon. Flute and oboe rest for the first fifteen bars, and the horn enters at p in bar 9.
cues.evidence: Carl Nielsen Edition, series II, vol. 11, Chamber Music 2 (Edition Wilhelm Hansen, Copenhagen, 2003), Quintet, Op. 43, second movement, with the bar numbers printed there: https://www.kb.dk/dcm/assets/cnu/pdf/CNU_II_11_chamber_music_2.pdf, pp. 121–122, bars 1–16.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Written in Gothenburg, 1922
cues.text: Nielsen began the Quintet before leaving for Gothenburg in February 1922 and wrote the rest there, living with Herman and Lisa Mannheimer. The first movement was finished at the end of March, the second and third within a month, and the work was played at the Mannheimers’ home on 30 April.
cues.evidence: Carl Nielsen Edition, series II, vol. 11 (2003), preface to the Quintet: https://www.kb.dk/dcm/assets/cnu/pdf/CNU_II_11_chamber_music_2.pdf, p. xxxv. Private performance of 30 April 1922: Catalogue of Carl Nielsen’s Works, CNW 70, https://www.kb.dk/dcm/cnw/document.xq?n=70

cues.title: Trio, bar 45
cues.text: The Trio begins at bar 45 and moves to F major. Oboe and clarinet carry the melody, and the flute enters at p in bar 48. The section ends at bar 71 on a pp chord under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Carl Nielsen Edition, series II, vol. 11, Chamber Music 2 (Edition Wilhelm Hansen, Copenhagen, 2003), Quintet, Op. 43, second movement, with the bar numbers printed there: https://www.kb.dk/dcm/assets/cnu/pdf/CNU_II_11_chamber_music_2.pdf, pp. 124–125, bars 45–71.

cues.title: Return of the Menuet, bar 72
cues.text: The Menuet returns at bar 72, written out in full. The clarinet plays the melody at mp over the staccato bassoon, as in the opening bars.
cues.evidence: Carl Nielsen Edition, series II, vol. 11, Chamber Music 2 (Edition Wilhelm Hansen, Copenhagen, 2003), Quintet, Op. 43, second movement, with the bar numbers printed there: https://www.kb.dk/dcm/assets/cnu/pdf/CNU_II_11_chamber_music_2.pdf, p. 125, bars 72–76.

cues.title: This side re-recorded, May 1936
cues.text: Four takes were made of this side, matrix 2CS 295. The first three date from January 1936, and the fourth, which was issued, was made on 5 May 1936.
cues.evidence: Take 4 of 2CS 295 and its date: The Gramophone Company Discography (after Alan Kelly), matrix 2CS 295, https://www.gramophonecompanydiscography.com/. The transferred side is listed as 2CS 295-4 in Internet Archive item db-5200-3-nielsen-wind-quintet-iii (description and label scans), https://archive.org/details/db-5200-3-nielsen-wind-quintet-iii.

cues.title: Coda, bar 115
cues.text: The Coda begins at bar 115 at f, with a rising run in the clarinet and a held note in the horn. In the last three bars all five instruments diminuendo together on repeated chords, marked rall., and the movement ends at bar 122 on a p chord under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Carl Nielsen Edition, series II, vol. 11, Chamber Music 2 (Edition Wilhelm Hansen, Copenhagen, 2003), Quintet, Op. 43, second movement, with the bar numbers printed there: https://www.kb.dk/dcm/assets/cnu/pdf/CNU_II_11_chamber_music_2.pdf, p. 128, bars 109–122.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Det Kgl. Kapels Blæserkvintet (Wind Quintet of the Royal Orchestra, Copenhagen) (ensemble), Holger Gilbert-Jespersen (flute), Svend Christian Felumb (oboe), Aage Oxenvad (clarinet), Hans Sørensen (horn), Knud Lassen (bassoon)
fields.note: The labels read “Det Kgl. Kapels Blæserkvintet. Gilbert Jespersen—Fløjte, Felumb—Oboe, Oxenvad—Klarinet, Kn. Lassen—Fagot & Hans Sørensen—Horn”. The Kelly files give the same five names, with Holger Gilbert-Jespersen in full, for the wind quintet of the Royal Orchestra, Copenhagen. The item description calls the ensemble the Wind Quintet of the Royal Danish Opera and says Gilbert-Jespersen joined in 1929; the Catalogue of Carl Nielsen’s Works lists him as the flautist at the Berlin performance of 29 March 1923, and Paul Hagemann as flautist at the first public performance on 9 October 1922.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Original version for flute, oboe, clarinet in A, horn in F and bassoon. The Menuet, the Trio, the written-out return of the Menuet and the Coda are present.
fields.note: The structure of the track (a Menuet, a Trio in F major, a return of the Menuet and a Coda) was compared with the printed bars of the Carl Nielsen Edition; no published list of the side was consulted. The label reads “2 Sats: Menuet”. Which score edition the players used is not stated.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Kelly files list matrix 2CS 295 with four takes: takes 1 to 3 are dated January 1936 without a day, and take 4, the issued take, is dated 5 May 1936. The item description gives 24 January 1936 for the set as a whole and lists this side as 2CS 295-4. The rest of the quintet was recorded on 24 and 25 January 1936.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The item description places the quintet sessions in Copenhagen, and the Kelly files give “Royal Orchestra, Copenhagen” as the ensemble. The place field in the Kelly files reads “Someplace, Scandanavia”, a placeholder, and no place is stated for the May take specifically. The studio or hall is not stated.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: His Master’s Voice (The Gramophone Company, Ltd.), 12-inch records in the Scandinavian red-label D.B. series, pressed in England
fields.note: The label scan reads “His Master’s Voice”, “Made in England” and “The Gramophone Co. Ltd.”, in Danish, with “Quintett” and the speed, 78. The item description calls DB 5200–5203 the first issue in the 12-inch Scandinavian Red Label series.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: HMV D.B. 5201 (side A), “2 Sats: Menuet”; the set is D.B. 5200–5203, 12-inch, 78 rpm
fields.note: Read from the label scan of D.B. 5201 A, which also carries a hand-marked side number 3. The Musical Quarterly of April 1937 lists the set as DB 5200–3, and The New Records of August 1937 as four 12-inch discs, DB5200 to DB5203.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: The label prints the matrix number 2CS 295 without a take; take 4 comes from the item description and agrees with the issued take in the Kelly files.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Internet Archive collection The Shellackophile’s Vintage Recordings; the person who made the transfer is not named in the item
fields.note: The item belongs to the collection described as recordings of classical music from the 78-rpm era. Photographs of the labels are included in the item; their photographer is not named.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.value: Not stated; the item was made public on 17 March 2022
fields.note: The public date of the item and the modification time of the uploaded FLAC file are the same day, which is an upload date and not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: One disc side of 4 min 28 s as one track. Equalisation, noise reduction and speed correction are not described.
fields.note: The movement is a single side, and the surface noise of the track is steady, with no join.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain. Nielsen died on 3 October 1931, so the work has been out of copyright in the European Union (life plus 70 years) since the end of 2001. The first edition was published by Wilhelm Hansen, Copenhagen, in 1923, which makes it public domain in the United States as well.
fields.note: The dates are documented; the legal conclusion is ours. The Carl Nielsen Edition of 2003, used here only for bar numbers and the preface, is a separate publication under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs 3.0 licence, and none of its text or music is reproduced.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: The set was listed as Danish Gramophone DB 5200–3 in The Musical Quarterly of April 1937 and reviewed as four 12-inch discs in The New Records of August 1937, so it was published by then. The uploader’s date of 1936 is not an independent source. The United States status of a Danish recording published in 1936 or 1937 is not established.

composer.born: 9 June 1865, Sortelung, Nørre Lyndelse, Funen, Denmark
composer.epithet: Danish composer, violinist and conductor, born on Funen and based in Copenhagen, who wrote six symphonies, the opera Maskarade, a wind quintet and a large body of songs and hymn tunes.
facts: Military bandsman in Odense, 1879–83 · Copenhagen Conservatory, 1884–86 (violin with Valdemar Tofte, theory with Orla Rosenhoff)
Second violin in the Royal Orchestra, 1889–1905 · conductor at the Royal Theatre, 1908–14 · conductor of the Music Society from 1915 · director of the Royal Danish Academy of Music from 1931
Symphony No. 1, 1894 · Maskarade, 1906 · Symphony No. 4, 1916 · Symphony No. 5 and the Wind Quintet, 1922
Six symphonies, two operas, concertos for violin, flute and clarinet, chamber and organ music, cantatas, and songs and hymn tunes for voice and choir

quote.text: The point is to be able to say a pure fifth in such a way that no one thinks he has heard that interval before.
quote.source: Carl Nielsen, quoted in the Dansk Biografisk Leksikon, “Carl Nielsen”; the occasion is not given there

composer.background:
Carl August Nielsen was born on 9 June 1865 at Sortelung, a cottage in the parish of Nørre Lyndelse on Funen. He was the seventh of twelve children. His father, Niels Jørgensen, was a house painter who played the fiddle at dances; he was known as Painter-Niels, and the children took Nielsen as their surname. At six, when he had measles, Carl was handed a three-quarter-size violin that hung on the wall, taught himself a few melodies and played them for his father. Emil Petersen, the assistant teacher at the village school, taught him to play from notes. Petersen later told how he had once passed Painter-Niels’s house and found a boy of seven or eight hammering on blocks of wood laid out as a keyboard.

Confirmed at fourteen, Nielsen was apprenticed to a shopkeeper whose business failed, and on 1 November 1879 he joined the band of the Sixteenth Battalion in Odense. In 1883 he showed a string quartet to Niels W. Gade in Copenhagen, and in January 1884 he entered the Conservatory on a scholarship, studying the violin and, with Orla Rosenhoff, theory and counterpoint. He left at the end of 1886. His Suite for Strings, Op. 1, was played at Tivoli on 8 September 1888, and in 1889 he joined the second violins of the Royal Orchestra, where he stayed for sixteen years.
